properties.decision: UNDECIDED. Raised by Anthony 2026-07-25 from his own situation: he is in Long Island, his brother is in Washington State, they want to work on one design at the same time and to see each other's projects. THREE ROADS, and the middle one is not the obvious winner. (a) GIT IS ALREADY THE CENTRAL SERVER — the design is a file in the repo, the repo already spans both coasts, and the claims layer that shipped 2026-07-25 already answers "who has what in hand" the moment either side pulls. Nothing to host, nothing to secure, nothing to pay for, and no new place for the design to live. What it cannot do is tell you about a claim before the other person pushes. (b) A HOSTED MCP over HTTPS — one server process holding the graph, both people's agents connecting to it, so a claim is visible the moment it is made and a design is reachable by someone who never cloned the repo. Costs: reflow2-mcp serves stdio only today (rmcp's streamable-HTTP transport exists, the binary does not use it), authentication does not exist at all, and it puts the design on a machine — which weakens but does not erase dec:repo-file-embedded's objection, since the machine would be Anthony's own droplet rather than a vendor's. (c) HYBRID — host a read/publish surface for reaching and browsing designs, keep writes local and merge through git, so the durable record never moves. THE CHEAPEST FIRST CUT, worth naming because it needs almost no core work: one server process PER PROJECT, each with its own graph path and its own token, and project selection becomes which URL the agent points at — no graph_id plumbing, no multi-tenancy, and a per-project blast radius if one goes wrong. A private tailnet instead of public TLS removes the authentication problem for exactly two people, which is the population this actually has.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 gain a hosted surface (one MCP over HTTPS) alongside the repo file?
properties.rationale: Held proposed, not built, because it sits against a decision made HOURS earlier on 2026-07-25 (dec:multi-writer-architecture: repo file plus merge on pull, no hosted service) and it must not be drifted into. Per dec:reopen-supersedes, the move is a NEW decision point rather than flipping that one back to proposed. What is genuinely new, and the reason this is not a rerun of the same argument: that decision answered "how do two writers avoid clobbering each other", and its rationale turned on concurrency being hypothetical and on not putting the user's design on someone else's machine. Neither objection addresses what was raised now — two machines that never share a filesystem, several projects per person, and wanting to READ and contribute to a design without cloning its repo. It is also the second field-sourced trigger in two days on the same seam, which is what cap:revise-trigger exists to notice; that it arrived by conversation rather than by detector is a finding about the detector, not about the trigger. THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded so nobody has to rediscover it: reflow2's loop is ask-the-human-and-record-the-decision, which is deliberate, attributable and slow — a shared live server optimises for simultaneity, which this tool does not need and may be harmed by. The thing the two of them described wanting is mostly non-colliding parallel work plus visibility, and git plus the claims layer already delivers most of that. What it does NOT deliver is the publishing case, and that is the strongest argument on the hosted side.

properties.decision: Requirement certainty is a computed reading, never a stored third axis: status accepted/met → user-confirmed; status deferred/dropped → settled out (also the user's word); status proposed → asserted (provenance authored/planned/imported) or recovered (provenance inferred/reconciled/healed). The load-bearing doctrine: an agent captures requirements at proposed and ONLY the user's answer moves the status — accepted, met, deferred and dropped are all user-only verbs. Reports render the certainty breakdown directly so no session reconstructs it in prose.
properties.name: A Requirement's certainty is derived from status × provenance; every move off proposed is the user's word
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-75 vocabulary session, from their fleet trial: where-am-i had to caveat user-confirmed vs recovered in prose every session). Derived over stored for the BL-73 reason — a third stored property can contradict the two axes that already span the space, and the backlog's own warning was 'decide deliberately, not additively'. Every-move-off-proposed rather than accepted-only because an agent dropping a requirement on its own judgment is exactly the silent decision the loop exists to prevent — and this is BL-12 sketch idea 2's example made real ('a requirement moves to accepted only on the human's say-so'), enforced culturally in the skills and the tool description today; the mechanical half stays with BL-41. 'Recovered' over the trial's 'adopted' because it matches the graph's own vocabulary (cap:adopt: 'Recover a design from an existing system') and names the fact, not the workflow. No schema change: the whole defect was the read side — the second time this week (BL-73) the vocabulary was already sufficient and unread.

properties.decision: A capability's verification state is three-valued: verified (a passing check of its own), component_verified (no check of its own, but a component it is allocated to carries a passing one — computed at read time, never written), and unchecked. The coverage line reports the third state as its own clause; detect_gaps replaces the N per-capability unverified alarms with ONE component_granularity_verification gap per carrying component at 0.35 — listing the riding capabilities, acknowledgeable once; status_contradiction accepts component-granularity proof for a verified status claim; loop_status counts component_verified as proven. A failing component suite carries nothing: passing-is-verified holds at every granularity.
properties.name: Component-granularity verification is a computed third state, one question per component
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-73 vocabulary session, from their own fleet's field trial): a brownfield adopt with real per-service suites plus a 137-file integration suite read as '0/20 capabilities verified' and cost 21 near-identical acknowledge writes. Computed state over a bulk-attest write because the graph should record exactly what was checked — the component — and derive what that means one hop away; manufactured capability-level VERIFIES edges would be indistinguishable from direct checks forever after. The word component_verified because it says where the check lives. One gap per component because the residual question ('is component granularity enough for these?') is genuinely per-component and deserves to be asked once, not N times — the BL-42 lesson again: a loud detector needs a different question, not a tuned number. The write side needed nothing: VERIFIES accepts any target and even carries an unused coverage enum — the whole defect was the read side.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and recorded as BRAINSTORMING rather than as a proposal — Anthony's own framing, 2026-07-25, thinking out loud. His starting doubt is the right one and had not been written down: claiming a cluster of nodes says nothing about the REPOSITORY, and if the design and the code share one repo, two people working different clusters still collide in git even when they never touch the same node. FOUR IDEAS AS HE PUT THEM. (1) reflow2 REPLACES git — the graph defines who may touch what, and git becomes an internal implementation detail. (2) The graph is a set of TEMPORARY LOCAL repos, pushed upstream only once work is done and no conflicts exist. (3) Each session opens a TEMPORARY WORKTREE BRANCH holding an identical copy of the graph; the person works there, then reflow2's own merge reconciles the copy back and the temporary is deleted. (4) A WEBSOCKET pushing every change to every user, giving live simultaneous collaboration. WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, and it matters for ranking them: the collision is in the export FILE, not in the graph, and reflow2 already answers file-level collision semantically — BL-80's three-way merge compares per node and per property against the common ancestor and mints each real conflict as a Question with a deterministic id, and `--merge`/`--merge-apply` run it without a server. So idea 3 is not new machinery; it is mostly a PROCEDURE over machinery that exists, and a git worktree already gives each person their own checkout with its own `.reflow2/graph` (the store lock is per-directory). The missing piece is small and specific: git supports per-path merge drivers — this repo already uses `merge=union` for COORD.md — so registering the design export with a driver that calls reflow2's own merge would make two people working different clusters merge automatically, and make a genuine overlap arrive as a Question instead of as conflict markers in a 500KB JSON file. Idea 2 is idea 3 with extra steps, since git branches are already local until pushed. Idea 1 would make reflow2 a version-control system, contradicts dec:repo-file-embedded and req:persistence, and would have to reinvent what it currently inherits for free. Idea 4 is the simultaneity road already held open by dec:central-host and BL-99, with the counter-argument recorded there: this tool's loop is deliberate and attributable rather than live.
properties.name: OPEN — how are two people's simultaneous edits kept apart: worktrees, temporary repos, or a live channel?
properties.rationale: Held as brainstorming on purpose. Anthony called it thinking out loud, and the first honest thing to do with four ideas is to write them down as four ideas rather than pick one and start building — which is precisely the practice dec:exploratory-staging is about. Two notes for whoever takes it up. The ranking above is a finding, not a decision: it says which ideas are cheap and which are large, and the cheap one is testable this week by two people on one design without a line of new Rust. And the doubt that started it should survive into whatever gets built — a claim on a cluster of nodes is not a claim on a repository, so any answer here has to say what happens to the CODE two people are writing beside the design, not only what happens to the graph.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED. Anthony, 2026-07-25: COORD.md was invented so he and his brother could coordinate; the claims layer shipped the same day; and reflow2 is developed by using reflow2 on itself, so the question is whether the markdown board should now be a graph read. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE, because it is less than it sounds: `claim_region` records a Contributor holding a seed node to a depth, `claim_report` computes the region and the overlaps, and both travel in the committed export exactly as COORD.md travels in git — so visibility is unchanged, and the gain is that the region is COMPUTED from the design (it follows the graph as the design moves) rather than being a hand-typed list of file paths that goes stale silently. WHAT WOULD BE LOST, and it is the part worth deciding rather than assuming: COORD.md is readable by a human with no reflow2 and no binary, it shows up as a diff in a pull request, and it holds the merge-conflict doctrine for the shared records — none of which a graph read does. The sane split, if this is taken: claims in the graph for WHO HAS WHAT, COORD.md retained for the conventions and the conflict doctrine, and the in-progress table deleted rather than maintained in two places, since two places for the same fact is the failure the backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2's own claim board move from COORD.md into the graph?
properties.rationale: Raised as a dogfooding question, which is how most of this project's real findings have arrived — and it is a genuinely good test of the claims layer, because reflow2's own two-person collaboration is the only live multi-writer case that exists. Held proposed because a claim board is a coordination mechanism between two people, and switching it unilaterally would mean one of them silently changing where the other must look; that is Anthony's brother's call as much as his. The prerequisite is honest: nobody has used claim_region for real yet, so the first move is to run it on one real piece of work and see whether claim_report says something a person would have said.

properties.decision: ifc:core-api — the DesignGraph API cmp:graph provides and the MCP service consumes — is the sole operational path between the Design Store and the Agent Surface subsystems. Accepted as a SPOF, like dec:graph-spof-accepted and dec:service-spof-accepted.
properties.name: The DesignGraph API is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: One store, one surface over it (req:agent-native, single-writer storage): the bridge between them is inherently single. Surfaced when BL-83a retired cmp:core and moved the API's provider to cmp:graph; the topology is honest, not a defect to engineer away.

properties.decision: The design's authorship identity is a new first-class Contributor node type (kind: person / automated_agent / organization), kept separate from the existing Actor. Actor is who the designed system SERVES (boundary-facing domain content); Contributor is who authors and decides the design ITSELF. The first rung is the authorship seed: an AUTHORED_BY edge (any design node → Contributor, role author/reviewer/approver) — the structured "who" behind provenance's "how", replacing the free-text Requirement.source. AUTHORED_BY is deliberately NOT a traceability edge (absent from nodes.rs structural_rule), so authorship is metadata and never enlarges a blast radius. Later rungs, each needing the user on vocabulary: CLAIMS (BL-44 node/cluster claims, advisory-first), ACTS_FOR (agent-acts-for-person, git's author/committer split), alternative-authorship (BL-70), and signing the export content_hash with a Contributor key (BL-41 mechanical half). No "unauthored node" detector yet — it would N-alarm on every existing node.
properties.name: Design-authorship is a Contributor, distinct from an Actor; the seed is AUTHORED_BY
properties.rationale: User chose the identity keystone as the next most important work (2026-07-22), and decided both axes: a new type over overloading Actor, and authorship-first over jumping to claims. First-class node over a bare property because a claim expires and authorship belongs on axis-Z — a property is invisible to history. One identity mechanism because the backlog's own warning is that building it for claims alone would be "the recurring lesson in reverse": the same who-is-this is needed by BL-44 (claims), BL-70 (alternative authorship), BL-41 (the mechanical half of requirement-certainty, cultural today), and BL-12 sketch 2 (who may assert what). Contributor separate from Actor because they have different lifecycles — a UAF model keeps who-serves and who-makes apart. The git exploration (2026-07-22) independently ratified the shape: git's author-vs-committer split is exactly the deferred ACTS_FOR rung, and signing the record hash is BL-41's mechanical half. Additive schema change (28 node / 55 edge types); a new-binary graph is refused loudly by a pre-Contributor binary via the count-based provenance check (BL-19), so no schema_version bump.

properties.decision: A design-vs-design diff (compare_designs) exists as a core op exposed as both an MCP tool and a CLI flag. It compares two export documents, or the live graph against one document. Findings are directional — added / removed / changed relative to an explicitly named base — with property-level detail on changed nodes, grouped into two bands: design content vs the supporting/bookkeeping layer (ChangeEvents, DriftEvents, Fragments, Questions). It reports divergence between two as-designed records and never judges which side is right; the word 'drift' stays reserved for design-vs-reality.
properties.name: Design-vs-design comparison is directional, banded, and lives in the core
properties.rationale: User decided all four axes 2026-07-21 (BL-71 rung c vocabulary session). Directional because all three consumers have a real base — the committed record (the BL-71 clobber tripwire), the main branch (BL-70 branch-by-file comparison), the state a claim was made against (BL-12 merge) — while AoA can still read the report neutrally or run it both ways. Banded because the real 2026-07-21 divergence was 3 Decisions and 8 Requirements buried under ~20 bookkeeping nodes; a flat list hides exactly what matters. Core op (not a kit script) because deterministic design computation belongs in the tested core; CLI flag so CI and no-server contexts reach it, like --import/--export. It is the read side of the rung a+b upsert-layering, the sibling of the reconcile family — which compares design against reality, hence the separate word: divergence, not drift.

properties.decision: The Documentation subsystem, its docs component, the capability of explaining reflow2 to a newcomer, and the README/SETUP artifacts read as a disconnected community to `detect_defects`, and that reading is ACCEPTED rather than bridged. The cluster is correctly modelled: the project contains the subsystem, the subsystem contains the component, the component owns the capability, and the artifacts both REALIZE the capability and DOCUMENT the project, the installer and the service. Those DOCUMENTS edges are true and are kept on their own merit — the tool's own guidance is to record a file that way when something would be wrong if it drifted out of step with the design, which is exactly the property the user asserted when he said documentation is part of the deliverable. They simply do not attach the cluster, because the structural network is built from DEPENDENCY relations only (a direct DEPENDS_ON, or a CONSUMES/PROVIDES contract collapsed through its Interface), and documenting a thing is not depending on it. No further edge can fix this without being a lie: documentation genuinely does not participate in the operational dependency graph.
properties.name: Documentation is part of the product but has no operational coupling, so its island is accepted — and the detector should learn this
properties.rationale: Decided 2026-07-24, immediately after the user answered that documentation belongs to reflow2 rather than sitting outside it ("it'd be like if I designed a fighter jet using reflow2, but then didn't deliver any documentation on it to the user"). Three bridges were attempted before accepting: project containment, which is how every other subsystem attaches; then DOCUMENTS edges to the project, the installer and the service. The detector still fired, and reading structure.rs explains why — the design network admits a defined TRACEABILITY set (SATISFIES, ALLOCATED_TO, REALIZES, VERIFIES, GOVERNED_BY, PROVIDES/CONSUMES, DEPENDS_ON, INCLUDES) and DOCUMENTS is simply not in it, while CONTAINS is deliberately excluded. That selectivity is correct and should not be weakened to silence this. THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, which is why this is worth recording rather than shrugging at: dec:operational-spof already established that only things which OPERATE can be single points of failure, because the suggested fix — add redundancy — is meaningless for intent. The identical argument applies one category over. Only things that operate can be meaningfully disconnected FROM the operational network; a documentation subsystem has no operational coupling by its nature, so flagging it is a false positive of the BL-84 family, and the fix belongs in the detector rather than in the design. RESOLVED 2026-07-25, and NOT by the fix this decision anticipated — recorded because a decision that goes on claiming to accept something that no longer happens is exactly the drift this project exists to catch. The island dissolved on its own when cap:session-memory turned out to belong to BOTH cmp:docs and cmp:temporal: the user's point that a session's context is itself documentation gave documentation a genuine, non-cosmetic tie to the rest of the design, through ALLOCATED_TO edges that are true rather than manufactured. So the detector was never wrong about the topology — the topology changed, because the design gained a real connection it had been missing. The PRINCIPLE above stands unaltered and still applies to any future documentation-only cluster; only the specific defect it dispositioned has gone. Worth keeping as evidence for the detector fix: an island can be legitimate AND later dissolve legitimately, so the exemption must not be written in a way that hides a genuine disconnection.

properties.decision: Standing rule for the edge vocabulary: two edge types must be orthogonal, because an LLM asked to choose between near-synonyms picks inconsistently (storyflow's lesson). The test for keeping any distinction is not 'is it true?' but 'does a computation — a detector, a report, a propagation rule — read the two sides differently?' If nothing reads it, the distinction is descriptive decoration that costs extraction consistency for no gain (the 'read side was blind' lesson turned on the vocabulary itself). Applied 2026-07-22: (1) RETIRE the VALIDATES edge — it was orthogonal-in-name-only with VERIFIES (both land Verification->Capability, the canonical V&V confusion) AND orphan (no core code ever referenced it). The verify-vs-validate distinction is real and worth keeping, so it moves to a Verification.kind property (verification | validation) — a property of the check, not a rival relationship, which removes the edge-choice ambiguity entirely — and it earns its keep via a new unvalidated_capability DETECT gap that reads it (a capability verified against spec but with no validation check confirming it meets intent). (2) FOLD ENABLES into CAUSES — same causal axis, differ only by degree (brings-about vs makes-possible), both wildcard-typed, and neither read by any computation; CAUSES's hint now covers the enabling case. (3) KEEP TRIGGERS — it is not a causal-degree variant: it carries a role property and drives the Flow/process-feedback model (flow_report, BL-37), so a computation reads it. Net: 55 -> 53 edge types; the 'does a computation read it?' test is the standing rule for any future edge.
properties.name: A vocabulary distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it; retire VALIDATES + ENABLES edges
properties.rationale: User raised it from the storyflow lesson that edge types an agent chooses between must be completely orthogonal, and reasoned each case by cost/benefit: keeping a distinction buys nothing over collapsing unless a computation reads it, and sharpening extraction hints only lowers the error rate on a distinction that still has no reader — it cannot make a same-axis distinction orthogonal. VALIDATES was the clearest case: confusable AND orphan (the engine runs entirely on VERIFIES). Moving it to Verification.kind is strictly better than a rival edge because verify-vs-validate is an attribute of one check, not two relationships — as an edge it forces the confusable choice every time; as a kind there is always exactly one edge (VERIFIES). But a kind with no reader is the same orphan relocated, so it is kept only because the unvalidated_capability gap reads it — the mission-assurance question 'built to spec, but is it the right thing?', which the user's domain cares about. ENABLES vs CAUSES had no reader (0 core files each), so sharpening hints bought only cleaner extraction of a distinction nothing uses; collapsing removes the error class. TRIGGERS was rescued from the trio because it genuinely has a reader (its process role). The gap follows the BL-73 anti-flood lesson: one project-level rollup ('N verified capabilities have no validation check'), acknowledgeable once, not N per-capability alarms.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED as a vocabulary question, but MUCH SMALLER than it looked, and the skill that tests it is BUILT (2026-07-25, the brainstorm skill). REFRAMED by Anthony the same day, and the reframe was the useful part: what he and his brother were asking for is not a staging GATE, it is a KIND. "I think I now realize what my brother's idea was trying to say — it is like a brainstorming session where you can work through ideas without committing to anything yet. These would be more like 'ideas' not yet fleshed out and could be held in the graph as just that, 'brainstorming ideas'." That dissolves the contradiction this decision was opened over: the git study rejected the index because a gate between every edit and the graph is where intent goes to be forgotten, whereas a brainstorm is the opposite move — the idea DOES enter the graph, immediately, labelled as what it is. Nothing waits outside, so nothing is lost, and the design still never claims a half-formed thought as intent. THE FINDING THAT SHRANK THE QUESTION, from reading the detector while building the skill: the existing vocabulary ALREADY tells a musing from a choice, and a computation already reads the difference. `detect_gaps` raises `undecided_decision_point` only on a proposed Decision holding TWO OR MORE REGISTERED ALTERNATIVES — a fork with a real design export behind each branch (detect.rs: `alts.len() < 2 { continue }`). A proposed Decision whose options live in its prose therefore raises NO gap at all. So brainstormed ideas are silent by construction, and the nudge to choose arrives exactly when the ideas stop being ideas: register_alternative turns an option into a fork, and being asked to decide a fork is correct. Nobody has to remember which is which, and no label was needed to get it. WHAT A `brainstorm` KIND WOULD STILL BUY, and it is now a short list rather than the four-item one recorded yesterday: (a) delivery and certainty counts already exclude Decisions, so nothing is owed there; (b) gap silence is already delivered, per the finding above; (c) what remains is RETIREMENT — an idea nobody has touched in months could be surfaced as a candidate for tidying rather than sitting in the decision list forever, which is a real computation and the only one left standing; and (d) READABILITY — a person scanning 70-odd Decisions cannot tell at a glance which were choices and which were musings, which the skill currently answers with a sentence of prose inside the node rather than with a queryable property. PRIOR FRAMING, KEPT because it was true when written: the ask read as an opt-in "think first, commit later" mode; a session making no write calls IS rubber-ducking and the read tools are the ducking aids; and the narrow question was what happens at the END — which the skill now answers as a PROMOTION step, not a commit step.
properties.name: OPEN — do half-formed ideas get a place in the graph, distinct from things the design asserts?
properties.rationale: Raised by Anthony and his brother 2026-07-24, reframed by Anthony 2026-07-25, and the skill built the same day on his word ("go ahead with the brainstorm skill"). Built as a SKILL and not a schema change deliberately: it tests the practice at the cost of prose, and if the practice sticks the vocabulary question can be answered with evidence instead of taste — whereas a new node type or an enum value would have bought an upgrade doc and a foundation-migration checklist for a noun nobody had used yet. The evidence for the feature is this session itself: Anthony produced four isolation ideas he explicitly did not want to commit to, and the only home for them was a proposed Decision. That worked (dec:concurrent-work-isolation), which is why this is not urgent; it is also a slightly wrong fit, since a Decision node is meant for a choice someone is actually facing, and knowing exactly which part of the fit is wrong is what the finding above now pins down. Left PROPOSED because two of the four original arguments for a kind have dissolved and the remaining two (retirement candidates, at-a-glance readability) are real but small — and whether they are worth a schema change is Anthony's call, not a judgement to be made by the agent that just wrote the skill.

properties.decision: cmp:export and ifc:graph-export are the only route from a design to the kit converter (cmp:init) and to any other machine or reflow2 version, and they stay that way. Both single_point_of_failure warnings are accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding a second export path.
properties.name: The export document is an accepted single door, so its chain is an accepted SPOF
properties.rationale: dec:repo-file-embedded made the deterministic export the durable, diffable record, and req:survives-upgrade makes export-with-the-old-build / import-with-the-new THE migration mechanism — a single door is the feature, because a second export path would be a second source of truth for what the design is, and byte-identical determinism (req:persistence: a backup under git shows what actually changed) is only a meaningful promise about one format. The detector is right that severing this chain cuts cmp:init off from the design; that fragility is the price of one canonical portability format, knowingly paid. Accepted 2026-07-21 while dispositioning BL-69's corrected findings; sibling of dec:service-spof-accepted and dec:graph-spof-accepted.

properties.decision: Every export carries a content_hash — sha256 over the canonical sorted JSON of the design content only (graph_id, nodes, edges), excluding the stamp and chain fields, so the same design hashes identically whichever build wrote it. A prev_content_hash records file lineage: when an export overwrites an existing export file, the chain advances to the old file's content hash — but only when content actually changed, so two exports of an unchanged design stay byte-identical. The full hash is carried (not truncated like display checksums) because this is tamper evidence. compare_designs reports ancestry from the chain (other succeeds base / base succeeds other / siblings of a common parent / unknown); import reports an integrity mismatch loudly; the CI gate fails on a committed export that does not match its own hash. Documents predating the hash stay importable and comparable — absence is reported, never an error.
properties.name: The export proves itself: content hash + file-lineage chain, from AT proto's self-authenticating repos
properties.rationale: User directed 2026-07-21 after the AT Protocol comparison: atproto repos are self-authenticating (signed commits over a content-addressed root), and reflow2's export was already deterministic — the hash was well-defined and simply never computed. Content-only hashing (stamp excluded) was proven necessary the same day: the committed export and the live export had identical content but different writers (0.8.0 script vs 0.7.0-era session server), and they must fingerprint the same. The chain lives at the file-write seam because the committed export file IS the durable record whose lineage matters; the graph itself must not be mutated by a read-only export. Ancestry is what turns compare_designs from 'what diverged' into 'was the divergence made in ignorance of the base or in defiance of it' — BL-12 sketch idea 1's question, computable for the one-step case. Signing (identity) is deliberately deferred until a second writer is real; a hash chain without keys is already tamper-evident against accident and hand-editing, which is today's actual threat model.

properties.decision: The FNV-1a id hash (fnv1a) moves from cmp:detect (detect.rs) to cmp:nodes (nodes.rs), the vocabulary/identity leaf everything already sits above. This breaks the critical detect↔verify circular dependency: detect→verify is a genuine domain dependency (gap detection reads a capability's verification state, crate::verify::CapabilityVerification), but verify→detect existed ONLY because verify borrowed crate::detect::fnv1a to mint a deterministic id — not a domain dependency at all. Relocating the primitive removes that false edge (cycle broken, one-way detect→verify remains) and, as the same true consequence, removes five more fnv1a-only false couplings on cmp:detect (agent, artifact, drift, fielded, heal → detect all had no other detect reference); cmp:report keeps its real detect dependency (crate::detect::GapCandidate). Net self-model reconciliation: −6 DEPENDS_ON→cmp:detect, +1 cmp:agent→cmp:nodes (agent's new, real dependency on the primitive's home).
properties.name: The deterministic-id hash is a foundational primitive in nodes, not a detection concern — break the detect↔verify cycle by relocating it
properties.rationale: User directed fixing the critical cycle (2026-07-23). BREAK over ACCEPT because the cycle was not a genuine mutual dependency to live with — it was an artifact of a homeless utility: fnv1a began in detect.rs (where gap-id hashing first needed it) and eight modules reached through crate::detect::fnv1a, so the graph asserted a dependency on the detect DOMAIN that the code did not really have. Accepting it would embalm that lie; the honest move is to put the primitive where it belongs. RELOCATE-to-nodes over introduce-an-interface or invert-a-dependency because minting a derived node's id (gaps, heal issues, merge conflicts, prompts, drift/artifact keys) is an identity concern, and nodes is the vocabulary/identity module that is already a dependency leaf (depends on nothing), so the primitive gains no new coupling and creates no new cycle — the minimal, truthful home. The build script derives DEPENDS_ON from source (never prose), so a future rebuild reproduces exactly this shape; the committed self-model was reconciled by hand this session because it carries live-only nodes (req:nudge-covers-bypass, req:read-surfaces-debt) that block a full rebuild. Sibling in spirit to dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition (structure follows function/reality, not the file tree's accidents). The remaining structural defects are all accepted SPOFs and genuinely-disconnected intent clusters; this was the one critical one.

properties.decision: "The design as it stood at decision D" resolves by a three-step address: the Decision is pinned AT_EPOCH to a DesignEpoch, that epoch's existing `checksum` property carries the content_hash of the export cut there, and the document itself lives where it already lives — a git-committed reflow2.json. reflow2 supplies the coordinate; git supplies the bytes. No new node type, no mutable pointers, no reflow2-native DAG. Re-taking a road home is then the three-way merge already built (dec:merge-three-way), with the fork point as the base — which is precisely the merge-base reflow2 currently borrows from git, now derivable from its own epoch chain.
properties.name: A fork point is a coordinate (decision → epoch → export hash), not a stored copy or a native ref layer
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24, choosing the coordinate over a native ref/branch layer. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: branch names as graph nodes — mutable pointers to epochs, a real DAG, so reflow2 finds its own merge-base without git. Rejected on two grounds. (1) It duplicates machinery git already provides, and dec:repo-file-embedded already put the design in the repo as a file precisely so the repo's tooling carries the file-shaped concerns; dec:merge-three-way already chose explicit inputs over git's DAG for the same reason. (2) A mutable pointer is a foreign object in this graph: the whole doctrine of axis Z is that history is never overwritten (req:intent-preserved, req:roads-not-taken), and a ref that moves is by construction a thing whose past value is lost unless separately recorded — reintroducing the erosion the epoch chain exists to prevent. The coordinate has the further virtue of costing nothing: DesignEpoch.checksum already existed in the schema, described as "a hash over the anchored spec set at this epoch", which is exactly this use. Honest limit: only exports from v0.9.0 on carry an embedded content_hash (dec:export-hash-chain shipped then), so epochs before it are addressed by git tag alone and claim no checksum rather than inventing one.

properties.decision: cmp:graph is the single store handle everything else hangs off, and it stays that way. The single_point_of_failure warning on it is accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding redundancy.
properties.name: The graph handle is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: The architecture is explicit (AGENTS.md): DesignGraph is 'the single handle everything else hangs off' — one schema-validated CRUD surface so every coherence-loop module speaks to one store one way. Removing it strands schema, search and vocabulary (each with its file) plus the export chain, which is the BL-69 detector telling the truth about the spine. Redundancy is incoherent here twice over: these are modules compiled into one binary (they cannot fail independently of cmp:graph at run time — the same reasoning as the F6 library filter, which cannot see cmp:graph only because it provides no Interface node), and a second graph handle would mean two write paths to one store, exactly the incoherence the single handle exists to prevent. Accepted 2026-07-21 while dispositioning BL-69's corrected findings; sibling of dec:service-spof-accepted.

properties.decision: loop_status reports what the coherence loop is owed — anchored gaps never surfaced, questions waiting or answered-but-unwritten, structural defects, capabilities claiming realized/verified with no passing check, drift awaiting disposition, claims never examined — computed entirely from current graph state. reflow2 does not track when tools were run: phase nudges are excluded (guidance, not debt), and the write tools carry static loop_hint pointers at the next loop step in their own results.
properties.name: Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history
properties.rationale: From the StoryFlow fleet trial (BL-74): under operational load the agent kept bookkeeping via raw tools while the loop skills silently stopped — 'a design-discipline tool that depends on being remembered will lose to operational urgency every time; fire on a trigger, not on virtue.' Run-history ('no detect_gaps since Tuesday') is not honestly computable here: the core takes no clock, and looking-is-not-writing is doctrine — recording reads so observation could be tracked would make looking mutate the record. Outstanding debt is the state-based equivalent and the actionable truth regardless of who ran what when. The hint rides the tool result the agent already reads (zero extra round-trip to see it), and loop_status is the cheap computation a client hook can fire on its own events — rung a of the BL-74 ladder builds on exactly this call. Decided 2026-07-21.

properties.decision: The three-way merge (cap:merge-designs, dec:merge-three-way) resolves per node, per property, and per edge against the base by this case table. NODES/PROPERTIES: only one side changed a property -> take it; both changed it differently -> conflict. add/add (same id, no base) -> treated as modify/modify against an empty base: matching properties merge, each differing property is a conflict. delete/delete -> node gone, no conflict. delete/modify (one side removes the node, the other changes it) -> RETAIN-AND-ASK: the proposal keeps the modified node and raises a conflict asking the human to confirm the deletion or keep it, leaning toward keeping — deletion is the destructive side and must be re-justified, never the silent default (req:intent-preserved, retire-vs-delete). Symmetric in both directions. EDGES: first-class design content and get the identical three-way rule — one-sided add or remove -> take it; the same edge changed differently on both sides, or one side removes while the other changes it -> conflict; never silently drop an edge one side deliberately cut (req:no-silent-fallback). CONFLICT REPRESENTATION: a both-sides conflict is a Question node with source 'merge_conflict', a deterministic id (FNV over base + node/edge id + property, the existing gap-id normalization), carrying the base/ours/theirs values; it reuses the existing answer_question / open_questions machinery and writes nothing until dispositioned, and its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung (BL-80 #5) replays a recorded resolution against. No new node type — the schema stays 28.
properties.name: The merge conflict case table: retain-and-ask on delete, edges symmetric with nodes, conflicts are Questions
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option, closing the sub-decisions dec:merge-three-way explicitly deferred. Retain-and-ask over a neutral conflict because losing a node is not symmetric with keeping it: req:intent-preserved and the retire-vs-delete distinction make a delete the move that must be justified, so the proposal keeps the node and asks rather than treating erasure as an equal default. Edges symmetric with nodes because they carry the golden thread — a lighter union-and-keep-wins rule would override a deliberate one-sided edge removal without asking, which is exactly the silent drop req:no-silent-fallback forbids; compare_designs already bands edge divergence, so the input is there. Reuse Question over a dedicated MergeConflict type for the recurring schema-minimalism reason (the vocabulary was already sufficient — same lesson as dec:certainty-derived and dec:component-verified-computed): the answer/open-questions machinery, the deterministic FNV gap-id normalization, and the human-decides routing all already exist, and reusing them makes the conflict rerere-ready for free (BL-80 #5) while keeping the schema at 28 node types. With this, the merge is fully specified — nothing left but the build and its verification.

properties.decision: reflow2 records how a human resolved a merge conflict and offers it back when the same conflict recurs (git's rerere), on three axes the user decided. (1) STORAGE — in the graph, as an answered Question (source=merge_resolution) whose id IS the conflict's content fingerprint: reuses the answer_question/open_questions machinery, travels with the design in the export, no schema change (stays 28 node types) — exactly what dec:merge-conflict-semantics anticipated ('reuse Question; its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung replays against'). (2) BEHAVIOR — advisory: a recorded resolution is surfaced as a suggestion on the matching conflict, and the human still confirms (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks). apply_merge applies only what it is given; an opt-in use_recorded lets the human bulk-accept every recorded suggestion in one move (the confirmation is passing the flag), and apply refuses if any conflict still has neither an explicit nor a recorded decision. (3) KEY — content only: the fingerprint is over (property, base value, ours value, theirs value), independent of which node, so ONE resolution replays across ALL nodes with the identical conflict — this is git's model and what delivers the motivating BL-73 win (20 near-identical conflicts, 21 near-identical hand-resolutions → resolve the shape once). apply_merge records every applied property/edge-property resolution keyed by content, so the memory grows as you work.
properties.name: rerere: record a conflict resolution content-keyed in the graph, replay it advisory-only
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option. Content-only keying because it is the whole point: the BL-73 field pain was N near-identical conflicts across different nodes, and a per-node key would give near-zero reuse and miss exactly that case; content-only is git's proven model, and pairing it with advisory behavior keeps over-reach visible (the human sees each application). Advisory over auto-apply because the three-party doctrine puts the decision with the human — but the recorded suggestion plus a bulk-accept toggle kills the repetitive grind without silently resolving on the human's behalf. Reuse-Question over a new node type or a side cache is the recurring no-schema-change lesson AND keeps the memory inside the design that travels in the export (a side rr-cache would be a second source of truth that a teammate importing the design would not receive). Scoped in v1 to property and edge-property conflicts (a clear base/ours/theirs value triple, and the N-near-identical shape); node-type and delete/modify keys are deferred (no clean value triple), as is aging/pruning the memory. Extends cap:merge-designs; the conflict ids the merge already mints were built for exactly this (dec:merge-conflict-semantics).

properties.decision: When HEAL merges DUPLICATES-asserted nodes, the survivor is picked by provenance rank (authored > planned > imported > reconciled > inferred > healed); node id breaks ties. Pre-provenance graphs are unchanged.
properties.name: Merge survivor is chosen by provenance, id breaks ties
properties.rationale: User decided option 2 for BL-29 (2026-07-20): provenance is the closest thing the graph has to 'who asserted this and how deliberately'. Refinement from the 2026-07-20 self-adopt live session: a node with UNSET provenance defaults to authored, which made two genesis stubs tie against authored+verified survivors and nearly win on alphabetical id — set provenance explicitly on both sides before proposing a merge, and consider ranking unset below authored in a future revision.

properties.decision: The design merge is a three-way typed merge exposed as a core op (MCP tool + CLI flag), the write-side sibling of compare_designs. (1) Inputs are three explicit export documents — a common ancestor (base), ours, theirs; git supplies the base (git merge-base + the committed reflow2.json at that commit), so reflow2 does not build its own commit DAG for this rung. The multi-parent/ref layer that would let reflow2 find its own merge-base is deferred to BL-70/#3. (2) The algorithm is git's trivial-merge case table run per node and per property against the base over typed values, not lines: only one side changed a property -> take it; both sides changed it differently -> a structured conflict. (3) It produces a merge proposal — auto-resolved one-sided changes plus a list of both-sides conflicts rendered as Questions ('node X.prop Y: base=A, ours=B, theirs=C — which?') — and writes NOTHING to the graph. The human dispositions the conflict Questions, then an explicit apply commits the merge. Compare reports and never writes; merge does the same until the human has looked.
properties.name: The three-way merge takes explicit inputs over git's DAG, and reports a proposal it never auto-applies
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, both the recommended option. Explicit-inputs-over-git because the exports are already git-committed (dec:repo-file-embedded) and git already tracks the merge-base — building a second DAG inside reflow2 would reimplement what git provides and contradicts 'export/import is the right-sized git bundle analogue' (BL-80's explicit do-NOT-import list). It keeps rung #1 shippable now and defers the ref/branch layer to where it belongs (BL-70). compare_designs already computes the typed per-property diff this consumes, so the input side is built. Report-a-proposal-never-auto-apply because a both-sides conflict IS a Question and the graph must not silently pick a side (dec:report-dont-judge, req:human-decides, req:no-silent-fallback); mirroring compare's read-only contract keeps the sibling honest, and the explicit apply is the disposition gate (dec:two-sided-accept's spirit — no silent write) without a staging area (BL-80 explicitly rejects the index). Typed per-node/per-property conflicts are strictly better than git's line markers — the key 'graph is not files' caveat. This specifies BL-12's merge problem: rung #1 (this algorithm over three documents) + #2 (the retained ancestor, here git's) = the L core of BL-12. Deferred to their own decisions: delete/modify and add/add conflict semantics (retire-vs-delete makes a delete meaningful, so delete/modify must go to the human, never auto-resolve), edge-merge banding, and the exact shape of the conflict Question.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, 2026-07-25, supplied the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook (OUSD(R&E) Systems Engineering and Architecture, February 2025, Distribution A) and was explicit about the frame: "just taking principles, concepts and ideas from this. not looking to implement mosa exactly over this document." So this records what the guidebook's concepts illuminate about reflow2, not a plan to become a MOSA tool. THE DEFINITION IT GIVES: "an acquisition and design approach consisting of a technical and business architecture that supports using system interfaces compliant with widely supported and consensus-based standards... A MOSA system structure allows for severable components to be incrementally added, removed, or replaced throughout the life cycle" (10 U.S.C. 4401, mandated for all DoD acquisition programs to the maximum extent practicable). ITS FIVE-STEP FRAMEWORK is a process, not a document: Plan, Modularize, Identify Interfaces, Define Interfaces, Standardize Interfaces — and reflow2 can already model a process rather than only a product (cap:model-process, Flow nodes), so the framework is expressible as a Flow whose steps the graph can be checked against. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS, from Table D-1 "MOSA Conformance Criteria and Verification Methods": most of what MOSA asks a program to demonstrate, reflow2 already computes for other reasons. Their MODULARITY criterion — "encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled, and organized into functional categories" — is the Leiden modularity score, community detection and the god-component detector that graph_report already prints. Their MOSA OBJECTIVES criterion — "demonstrate severable modular components" — is propagate_change: if the blast radius of a change inside a module stops at that module's interfaces the module is severable, and if it leaks past them the module is not modular whatever the architecture diagram says. That is severability as a COMPUTED property rather than an assertion, which is the same move dec:certainty-derived made for requirement status and cap:derived-completion made for delivery. Their MOSA MODULES criterion — "implement minimal functions, are functionally independent, encapsulated, and traceable to requirements" — is the god-component detector plus the golden thread. Their LIFE CYCLE CHARACTERISTICS criterion — severable, replaceable, interoperable, allowing competition — is the severability computation plus the alternatives layer, where interchangeable suppliers behind one interface are exactly an analysis of alternatives. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it is one vocabulary item and one check. (1) NOTHING MARKS AN INTERFACE AS KEY. MOSA's whole discipline turns on designating major/modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open; reflow2 has Interface nodes, provides/consumes and SPECIFIES, but no way to say "this one is the published boundary and that one is internal plumbing". BL-45 found the identical hole from the opposite direction — external dependencies between reflow2 projects — and recorded it as "nothing marks an Interface external-facing". Two independent routes to one missing property is the strongest evidence this design has for a vocabulary addition. (2) NOTHING CHECKS STANDARDS COMPLIANCE, and the vocabulary for it is present and unused: DesignRule is defined as a chosen standard or convention with an `enforced` flag, and there are zero DesignRules in any graph — the same schema-present-practice-absent shape as the temporal axis and the KPP vocabulary before them. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea rather than used to bury it: MOSA is domain vocabulary for defence acquisition, and req:design-anything says the vocabulary stays neutral. A MOSA conformance report is therefore a VIEW — a projection over computations that already exist, in the acquisition community's words — and not a set of new node types. Building it as a view keeps the core neutral (dec:views-are-projections) and any renderer fill-in remains a defect. If it were ever built as schema, reflow2 would have taken on one domain's language as its own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 report MOSA conformance, given it already computes most of the criteria?
properties.rationale: Recorded 2026-07-25 as brainstorming from the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook Anthony supplied, on his framing: principles and concepts, not an implementation of MOSA. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word ("let's promote both") into the two things the guidebook actually exposed as missing, both now accepted: req:key-interfaces (the design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read the distinction) and req:modularity-computed (severability and cohesion are computed from the graph, not asserted by the diagram). Both are GOVERNED_BY this decision. WHAT STAYS OPEN is the question this decision was opened on, and it is narrower now: whether reflow2 ships a MOSA-BRANDED report. The requirements are domain-neutral by construction — published boundary, severable part — so they can be built without answering it, and the acquisition community's words for the same criteria belong in a view over the computation rather than in the schema (dec:views-are-projections, req:design-anything). Deciding otherwise would adopt one domain's language as reflow2's own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning. SEQUENCING, and it is not arbitrary: req:key-interfaces comes first because req:modularity-computed depends on it — severability is only checkable once the design knows where a boundary is. req:design-composes also links through published boundaries, so the same property serves the federation thread; that is the second independent route to it, after BL-45 found the identical hole from the system-of-systems side on 2026-07-20.

properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25: the design STAYS a graph-in-a-repo-file, and many writers are handled by merging on pull. No hosted service, no shared writable store. Each person's design lives at ./.reflow2/graph in their own checkout, git moves it, and genuinely overlapping work is resolved by the three-way merge that already exists — typed per-node and per-property against the common ancestor, with each conflict minted as a Question carrying a deterministic id, and recorded resolutions replayable across near-identical conflicts (rerere). THIS CONFIRMS dec:repo-file-embedded RATHER THAN SUPERSEDING IT. That is the outcome worth noting: this was the first field-sourced re-opening of a settled decision, triggered because dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale said the concurrency argument was 'hypothetical while there is one writer' and fifteen developers made it concrete. The precondition genuinely changed, the decision was genuinely re-opened, and the original answer survived contact with the new evidence. A re-opening that ends where it started is not wasted — it converts an assumption into a tested position. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY. A HOSTED SERVICE: rejected on cost against confirmed intent, not on taste. It contradicts req:persistence ('the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo') and req:invocation ('the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project'), both accepted, so choosing it would have required retiring or revising confirmed intent rather than merely adding machinery. It also puts the design on a machine the user does not control, carries permanent operational burden, and breaks the session-transcript identity for everyone but the local user (a local path resolves for one person and silently misses for the rest). A HYBRID — hosted claims and presence over local designs: rejected as the weaker version of the same trade. It keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface to run, and buys live visibility that the claims layer can approximate without a server. WHAT THIS COMMITS TO BUILDING: the scoping primitive (BL-44 cluster claims) so two people do not collide in the first place, and merge-on-pull ergonomics. The honest weakness accepted with this choice: no live view of what others hold, so overlap surfaces at merge time rather than before it — which is exactly the trade git itself makes, and the one this project's users already understand.
properties.name: Many writers keep the repo file and merge on pull — no hosted service
properties.rationale: Raised by the user and his brother, 2026-07-24, from a concrete scenario rather than speculation. This is the first field-sourced trigger to re-open a settled decision, and it is worth recording WHY it counts as one: dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale reads "the service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer." Fifteen developers is that hypothesis arriving, so the decision is not being second-guessed — its stated precondition has changed. That is exactly the signal cap:revise-trigger is being built to surface automatically; here it arrived by conversation instead, which is itself evidence the trigger is worth building. Held proposed deliberately: the architecture question is upstream of every feature beneath it (req:concurrent-planning among them), and starting to build under an unmade decision is how a design acquires an architecture nobody chose. The counter-argument that belongs in the weighing, so it is not lost: reflow2's loop is built around asking a human and recording an attributable answer — deliberate, sequential, credited — and simultaneous editing may be the wrong shape for that product even where it is technically reachable. What the raised scenario actually asks for is non-colliding parallel work plus good merges, which may be reachable without a service at all.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, explicitly not convinced by the collaboration design and thinking out loud: "could you have small/mini reflow2 graphs inside itself... coming from a system of systems engineering approach, reflow2 may lay out the graph and how all the systems need to interact and where there are gaps, but what if we now had a mini-reflow2 graph for each system? And a mini-mini-reflow2 of the components in the system... the idea is that reflow2 has the tools to analyze the graph at each level and ensure there are no gaps and that it works with the higher level systems or system-of-systems." WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, because it changes what the idea is asking for. Levels exist and are already checked: Component.level is an enum of component / subsystem / system / system_of_systems / enterprise, CONTAINS between Components is the axis-Y spine, and hierarchy_issues already reports level_mismatch, missing_intermediate_level and orphan_level — the carburetor-to-body problem, imported from chain_reflow's matryoshka insight (docs/three-axes.md). And the multi-graph primitive exists unused: every node and edge carries graph_id, pinned to the constant "reflow2". So the question is not whether reflow2 can express nesting. It can. The question is whether a level should be a SUBTREE of one graph or a GRAPH OF ITS OWN. THREE OPTIONS. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL — today's shape. What is missing is not nesting but SCOPING: no read takes a subtree as its subject, so detect_gaps and graph_report always answer for the whole design. Adding a scope argument is a filter, not an architecture, and it delivers most of what was asked — the tools analysing each level. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM, COMPOSED — Anthony's idea. It buys four things one graph cannot: an independent write lock per system, which is a different and stronger answer to the collaboration problem than region claims, because separate graphs are PHYSICALLY separate where a claim is only advisory; an independent lifecycle, so a subsystem can be released, adopted or handed to a vendor on its own; selective publishing, which is exactly req:design-reachable-without-the-repo; and per-level scale, since detectors run over hundreds of nodes instead of tens of thousands. (c) A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY, LEVELS INSIDE EACH — the hybrid, and the shape federated systems engineering actually uses: you split where AUTHORITY splits, not where the hierarchy happens to have a layer. THE FOUR HARD PARTS of (b), each one real: the golden thread cannot cross a store boundary, because the schema validates both endpoints of every edge — so a parent's Component pointing at a child's design needs a typed COORDINATE (graph id + node id + the export's content hash at the moment the reference was made), which is precisely the choice dec:fork-point-address already made for fork points over a native ref layer. Gap detection goes blind at the seam: a parent requirement whose satisfying capability lives in a child graph would fire unsatisfied forever unless the child's evidence rolls up — and that roll-up is cap:derived-completion's computation applied one level higher, which is encouraging rather than novel. Freshness becomes load-bearing: a parent's view of a child is a claim about a VERSION of that child, so it is a dated examined claim and never a live truth (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). And the seam becomes the new collision point: two people changing the interface across the boundary still collide, now in the one place with no merge machinery. THE TENSION WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the opposite destination — "one graph the whole company plans in", with the CEO's objectives at the top and everything tracing upward. Federation and one-big-graph cannot both be the end state, and nothing in the design has ever chosen between them. THE DISCRIMINATOR, offered as a finding and not a decision: depth alone does not justify a separate graph. Nesting three levels of graphs costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check at every seam, and buys nothing that a scope filter would not have delivered — unless something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED. Where those hold, a graph of its own is right. Where they do not, it is ceremony.
properties.name: OPEN — one graph with levels, or a graph per system composed into a bigger one?
properties.rationale: Recorded 2026-07-25 because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design, and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word ("let's promote both"): the brainstorm produced two accepted requirements and stays open on the mechanism, which is the split that keeps both halves honest. req:analyse-at-any-level is the part he needed day to day and is ALREADY DELIVERED by cap:scoped-analysis (option (a), built first because it forecloses nothing). req:design-composes is the federation intent — a system's design as a unit that composes through interfaces — GOVERNED_BY this decision, so nothing gets built toward it until the mechanism is chosen. THIS DECISION THEREFORE STAYS PROPOSED, and that is not hedging: promoting an idea to intent is not the same act as choosing between three architectures, and collapsing this one would assert a shape Anthony has never chosen. Its options and the four hard parts of federation are unchanged above. The discriminator recorded then still stands as the thing to test when it is decided: depth alone does not earn a separate graph — ownership, separate release, or separate sharing does. NOTE FOR WHOEVER COLLAPSES IT: docs/org-scale-vision.md still records the opposite destination (one graph the whole company plans in), and req:design-composes now sits in the graph as accepted intent pointing the other way. That tension is real, on the record, and undecided; it is the strongest reason this decision should be made deliberately rather than discovered.

properties.decision: Parallel alternatives (an analysis of alternatives held open until a decision) are represented BRANCH-BY-FILE: each alternative is a separate exported design (a git branch's reflow2.json, or an export file), not a world-tag inside one live graph. This reuses everything BL-80 built — cross-branch comparison is compare_designs, collapsing the winner is merge_designs/apply_merge, retiring the loser is retire-from-design — so reflow2 owns almost no new branch machinery, consistent with the merge's 'git is the DAG' decision. Semantically, alternatives are design SPACE, not time: sibling alternatives coexist 'now' and CONTRADICT each other, held under a proposed Decision (the decision point) until it collapses — distinct from an epoch (EVOLVES_INTO, before->after). Forking is not advancing time; storage may still be a ref/epoch, but the semantic layer keeps 'the road not taken' apart from 'an earlier version' (BL-70's warning). v1 is the N-way AoA report (analyze_alternatives): measures per branch (graph_report snapshot — nodes, open gaps, allocation health, verification coverage) side by side, plus each branch's structural divergence from a named baseline (compare_designs). Rung 2 wires the decision point: a proposed Decision GOVERNS lightweight alternative pointers that CONTRADICT their siblings; collapsing accepts the Decision, merges the winner into the baseline, and retires the losers with their rationale.
properties.name: AoA alternatives are branch-by-file and live in design-space (CONTRADICTS), not time (epochs)
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, each the recommended option. Branch-by-file over world-scope because BL-80 already built the comparison (compare_designs), the collapse (merge/apply_merge) and the retire machinery, so branch-by-file is the cheapest increment BL-70 itself named ('one exported graph per alternative plus a cross-export comparison report ... branch-by-file works today') and it is consistent with dec:merge-three-way's 'explicit inputs, git is the DAG'; world-scoping would bake world-awareness into every detector (possible_duplicate, allocation, SPOF, …) — a large invasive change for a simultaneous-in-one-graph benefit not yet needed, and BL-70 says branch-by-file 'teaches what the real scoping primitive must preserve' first. Space-over-time because an AoA holds both roads at once (design space, CONTRADICTS); reusing the epoch/PRECEDES time chain for branches (git's literal branch=commit-in-a-DAG, BL-80 #3) would make the road-not-taken indistinguishable from an earlier version — exactly the conflation BL-70 warns against. This is the fork/navigation substrate BL-81 (roads-not-taken) needs and shares the scoping primitive with BL-44 (cluster claims). Deferred: the decision-point pointer nodes + collapse wiring (rung 2), world-scoping if simultaneous in-graph AoA proves needed, and per-branch readiness scoring (BL-68).

properties.decision: RESOLVED 2026-07-24 on Anthony's word: OPTION C. A read carries a loop-debt pointer ONLY when loop_status would report real outstanding debt, and stays silent when the loop is clean — never the static-every-read of (B), which BL-90 already rejected as boilerplate the agent learns to skim. AXIS 2 resolved: the hint rides the orientation-shaped reads (graph_report, scan_nodes, search_design, get_node — what an agent runs to get its bearings), and fires only when the owed-set CHANGES since it was last surfaced (fire-on-change) — so it appears once when debt arises and stays quiet until the picture moves, which also bounds the per-read cost of computing what is owed. The read-side sibling of the write tools' loop_hint (dec:loop-status-state-not-history). Satisfies req:read-surfaces-debt; unbuilt until it lands in the MCP read tools' result path. Options weighed: (A) do nothing — SessionStart + Stop suffice; (B) static reminder on every read; (C, CHOSEN) state-derived conditional hint.
properties.name: Reads surface loop debt only when it's real — option C (state-derived, orientation reads, fire-on-change)
properties.rationale: Leaning C on axis 1, for reasons already on the record. (B) is the failure mode the user explicitly rejected in BL-90 ("aggressive wording across ~90 tool descriptions — cancels out at that scale"): boilerplate on every return trains the agent to skim past it, and reads differ from writes in a way that makes static wrong here — a write always advances the loop (it creates debt, so a static "next step" is always relevant, which is why the write-side loop_hint is static and accepted), whereas a read creates no debt, so a constant reminder is irrelevant most of the time and becomes noise. (C) respects dec:loop-status-state-not-history (debt is computed from current state, never remembered) and dec:anchored-first (a real, named problem outranks a generic nudge). (A) is the honest null option: the three existing triggers may already be enough, and the marginal value of C is specifically the mid-session read that SessionStart and Stop don't see. Axis 2 exists because loop_status is cheap but not free; the throttle is where C's cost is paid. Sibling of the write-side loop_hint; BL-74 family. Awaits the user's word on both axes before anything is built to satisfy req:read-surfaces-debt.

properties.decision: When a past decision is re-opened to take a different road, the original Decision stays `accepted` untouched, and a NEW `proposed` Decision is created that OBSOLETES it and holds the alternatives (including the road originally taken, now a sibling rather than the incumbent). The decision-point machinery already built (register_alternative / alternatives_for / collapse_decision, and the undecided_decision_point gap) applies unchanged to the new node, because it is a genuinely open choice. The record therefore shows both that the question was settled and that it was later re-asked, with the reasoning of each visible in its own node.
properties.name: Re-opening a settled choice mints a new Decision that obsoletes the old one; the accepted Decision is never un-accepted
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: flip the original Decision's status back to `proposed` and hang the new alternatives on it — simpler, and reuses the existing node. Rejected because it overwrites the fact that the choice was ever settled: a reader of the graph afterwards sees an open question and cannot tell it was once answered, or when, or on what grounds. That is the ADR failure mode this whole system was built against (dec:two-sided-accept, "silent drift-accept does not exist"), and it would make the strongest evidence for re-opening — that we chose X, lived with it, and the trials found the hole — the very thing the re-opening erases. Snapshots would in principle preserve it, but only if one was taken, which makes the integrity of the record contingent on remembering a second step. Superseding is unconditional. It also composes with the existing vocabulary rather than straining it: OBSOLETES already means "retired on the record, not deleted" (the retire-from-design exit), and the new node's own `alternatives` obituary is written by collapse_decision when the re-opened choice closes, so the second decision documents the first without rewriting it.

Articulation-point analysis of the component/interface dependency graph (2026-07-21 self-host review) confirms cmp:service is a genuine cut vertex — removing it disconnects the MCP surface — so the finding is true, and the right disposition is to accept it rather than fix it. Contrast cmp:flow, flagged by the same detector but NOT a cut vertex (BL-69). Redundancy is the wrong fix; this SPOF is the architecture working as intended.

properties.decision: Every epoch on the retrospective chain corresponds to a real shipped release with a real git tag and date (v0.4.0 through v0.10.1), plus the pre-existing genesis and post-v0.5.0-hardening epochs. Each Decision is anchored to the epoch of the earliest release whose committed export actually contains it — evidence from the repo, not reconstruction from memory. Each Release is pinned to its own epoch. Epochs before v0.9.0 carry no checksum, because their exports predate the hash chain; they say so in their description rather than claiming one. Going forward, an epoch is cut as work happens so nothing needs backfilling again.
properties.name: The epoch chain is backfilled from shipped releases only — real tags, or nothing
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24 among three options. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVES: (a) forward-only — anchor from today and leave the past alone. Rejected because all 34 existing decisions are the ones actually worth re-opening; a fork layer that can only fork decisions made after it was built is a fork layer with nothing to fork. (b) full reconstruction — invent an epoch per work session across the whole history and synthesize the missing snapshots. Rejected because most of those boundaries are guesses, and a fabricated epoch is worse than an absent one: it looks like evidence. Release tags are the natural resolution because they are the only points in this project's history that are independently attested (a tag, a date, a published binary, a committed export), and because "the design as of the release that shipped it" is the question a fork actually asks. The cost is deliberately accepted: the 9 founding decisions anchor to v0.4.0, the earliest tag carrying an export, which is their earliest EVIDENCE rather than their origin — recorded as such in that epoch's description instead of being silently presented as the date they were made. FOUND WHILE DOING THIS: reflow2's own temporal axis was nearly unused — zero Snapshots, 8 of 42 ChangeEvents pinned, no Decision anchored at all, the chain stopped four days back — because add_change_event (cheap, epoch-free) had been used throughout where record_change (pins and snapshots) was meant. The fork layer's foundation was missing, not merely its ref layer.

properties.decision: Every capability is designed as a check one party places on another; none does another's job.

The deterministic core computes, the graph carries claims and their audit trail, questions route judgment to the human. docs/partnership.md maps each known LLM failure mode to its mechanism. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam).

Build nothing today that forecloses growing into a hosted, multi-user, multi-project service
properties.statement: Anthony's reframe, 2026-07-25, of what to do with the GitHub-MCP study's larger lessons: rather than hold them as a roadmap of features to build, hold them as a rule about what NOT to do now — do not take a shortcut today that would make it impossible for reflow2 to become what GitHub's MCP server is. A roadmap ages badly and gets stale in a document nobody reads; a non-foreclosure rule is checkable at the moment of the decision that would break it, which is the only moment it matters. THE SPECIFIC FORECLOSURES, from reading github-mcp-server (each one a shortcut that is tempting precisely because there is one writer today): (1) IDENTITY IN A GLOBAL. Authority must arrive with the caller and be read from the request, never stashed in a process-wide variable or resolved once at startup — GitHub constructs a fresh server per request in stateless mode for exactly this reason, and their lockdown cache carries the warning that a viewer-scoped lookup shared across requests runs under the wrong user's credentials. (2) INVENTING AUTHORITY. reflow2 must never become the thing that decides who may read what; it delegates to an authority that already exists, on GitHub's stated principle that a server must not let anyone reach more than they could reach without it. Building an account system would foreclose that by making reflow2 the authority. (3) TREATING THE SINGLE-WRITER LOCK AS A CONTRACT. One RocksDB handle is an implementation fact; the day it is a promise in a tool description or a skill, concurrency becomes a breaking change rather than a build. (4) CONFIG THAT WIDENS. Per-request configuration must only ever NARROW what the deployment allowed — GitHub's headers can restrict within static bounds and can never re-include what was excluded, and any read-only surface that a header can talk out of read-only was never read-only. (5) ONE GRAPH ASSUMED EVERYWHERE. graph_id already exists on every node and edge and is pinned to a constant; code that assumes the constant rather than reading the field is the foreclosure, not the constant itself. (6) TRUSTING TEXT BY ITS LOCATION. Once a design can arrive from someone else, text is untrusted because of where it came from, not because of which field it sits in — so the trust boundary belongs at ingress, before anything reads it. WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT: it is not a licence to build the hosted service, and not a reason to add abstraction now. Every item above is a constraint on shortcuts, satisfiable by writing the simple version carefully — the point is that the simple version stays a strict subset of the eventual one, so nothing has to be undone. ENFORCEMENT DECIDED 2026-07-25 (Anthony: "go with your recommendation"): ADVISORY, `enforced: false`, and deliberately so. VIOLATES_RULE is a vocabulary item no detector reads, so declaring this gate-blocking would promise a check that does not exist — the exact failure the KPP work was built to end ("a KPP that nothing checks is a comment"). The rule is the project's rule, confirmed by its author; the flag says only that no build has been stopped by it yet. It flips to enforced the day a detector can read a foreclosure from graph state — the honest first candidate being (4) and (5), which are mechanically checkable, unlike (2), which is a judgement about architecture.
